newsitem.title: USA: Maystadt sees big IMF role after euro launch.
newsitem.headline: Maystadt sees big IMF role after euro launch.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund will have a major responsibility to oversee the orderly transition to a new world monetary system that will come with the advent of the euro, the head of the IMF's policy-making Interim Committee said Monday.

"With the advent of the euro, the international monetary system will probably move from a dollar-denominated system to a new system with two or three reserve currencies -- the dollar, the euro and the yen," Philippe Maystadt, who is also Belgium finance minister, told an IMF conference here.
"The Fund will have the major responsibility to oversee the orderly transition to this new system," Maystadt added.
Specifically, the IMF will need to provide a safety net against the risks of wild fluctuations by the euro, he said.

"One will have to make sure that the Fund provides a safety net against the risks of excessive exchange rate fluctuations, not only with regard to the dollar and the yen ... but also with regard to the euro," Maystadt said.
That should be the case even if the European Monetary Union does not become a member of the IMF, he said.

He said the launch of the euro -- which is scheduled for 1999 -- will pose a variety of questions for the IMF, including the composition of the special drawing right, the IMF's artificial currency, and the Fund's oversight of EMU member countries and policies.
"I believe the EMU members will remain individual members of the Fund at least during a transition period," Maystadt said, rather than having the Union become a member on its own.
That, though, will raise questions about the IMF's relations with both EMU member countries and the EMU itself.
One question, he said, would be whether the IMF could assist the Euro region as a whole if EMU is not a member of the Fund.
While any request by EMU members for IMF credit is arguably very unlikely, the question is nevertheless an important one, Maystadt said.
The IMF will also need to review the currency composition of the SDR after the advent of the euro, he said.
The SDR is currently made up of a basket of currencies comprising the U.S. dollar, the mark, the French franc, the yen and the pound.

"With the creation of EMU it is very likely that at least two of these currencies will disappear," Maystadt said in an apparent reference to the mark and franc. "Therefore, the currency composition of the SDR will need to be reviewed."
